title: The method came back to the client
dek: Loopy stopped feeling like a side project when it changed how I approached a live StickerGiant problem.
body: StickerGiant needed a better way to explain how material, lamination, shape, border, and bleed change a sticker.
I used the loop I had been building in Loopy: ground the brief, make three genuinely different directions, render them, and check them on desktop and mobile.

One direction anchors the visualizer in the gallery. Another separates product photography from preview mode. A third teaches border and bleed side by side. None of them pretends to calculate price or produce a real proof.
AI made the options real enough to discuss. My job was deciding what each option needed to teach and where the prototype had to admit that it was only a prototype.

title: I started testing the whole loop
dek: A clean demo tells me almost nothing about whether a client can trust the product.
body: I ran Loopy from design-system setup through brief, directions, concept selection, build, review, and the next decision. Then I tested the awkward states: a missing source, a stale job, a broken credential, and an iteration pinned to old design rules.

The failures were more useful than the happy path. They led to immutable design-system snapshots, safer recovery, clearer empty states, and a setup that could be rebuilt locally without mystery credentials. Those repairs showed me what I still needed to prove before asking a client to trust it.

title: A design system needs a story and a source trail
dek: Tokens are not enough if nobody can see what they mean or tell whether they came from a real source.
body: I added Storybook so Loopy's foundations, primitives, and components could be inspected as a real system rather than a pile of values. I also taught Loopy to reject source-generated systems that contained no useful evidence.

A Figma link, a website, or a Storybook catalog now leaves a source trail. Loopy shows what it found, what it inferred, and what is still missing. A hollow token file no longer passes as finished work. When a client asks why something looks the way it does, I can point back to the evidence.

title: Security became a design problem
dek: A useful agent can also become a very efficient way to mishandle client work.
body: A security review found places where untrusted project content and powerful agent tools crossed the wrong boundary. I stopped treating that as somebody else's backend problem.

We tightened the runtime, reduced what agent processes could read, improved key handling, and made failure states close when something went wrong. If I want clients to put real product context into Loopy, protecting that context is part of the experience.

title: I stopped making users translate their design system
dek: The product should do the archaeology before it asks a designer to fill in the gaps.
body: Loopy's first design-system setup asked too much of the person using it. I changed the flow to start with evidence from Figma, a website, or a published Storybook, then show what was found and what was still uncertain.
I also replaced agent nicknames with role titles such as senior designer, principal designer, and UX researcher. Clients should not need our internal lore to understand who is doing what.
The lesson was annoyingly obvious: clever systems feel simple only when the system carries the translation work.

title: The loop moved into the conversation
dek: I wanted Loopy to begin where product decisions already happen, not in another empty dashboard.
body: I drew the core Buzz experience in Pencil, then built a local Loopy agent with its own Hermes profile and strict approval gates.
A synthetic channel thread became a brief, three directions, a human choice, a small test, and evidence returned to the same thread.

In that local test, a synthetic participant recovered the problem, chosen direction, and next decision without rereading the source conversation. The test also exposed an ambiguity between the next decision and later questions, so I changed the canvas.
I kept that correction in the next version. The prototype gave me something observable to improve.

title: Pencil became part of the build loop
dek: The design file stopped being a picture of the idea and became the source for the next implementation decision.
body: I reorganized Loopy's iteration flow in a Pencil file. The useful part was not the drawing itself. Agents could inspect the actual nodes, compare them with production, and turn the differences into an implementation contract.

The resulting stage kept the current work in the middle, the active role at the top, and the complete loop visible below. We built it, tested it, found places where the first implementation lost review behavior, and corrected them. Pencil gave me a design surface I could steer and a faster path into working software without pretending the first pass was right.

title: The agents' work became the interface
dek: A flow diagram was explaining Loopy while hiding the only thing worth watching.
body: I had given the pipeline too much screen. It showed that agents were busy, but not whether their work was any good. I minimized the diagram and made the live brief, research, concepts, critique, and decision the center of the page.

Brief Studio replaced a long form with a guided conversation. The research gate let me steer before concepts were generated. Resume logic kept a slow build from restarting every time the worker hiccupped.
Clients do not need a theater of agents. They need to see the work, understand the current decision, and know where to intervene.

title: The demo had to survive Monday morning
dek: Loopy was becoming a product, which meant the boring failures were now design material.
body: I moved Loopy from a local control loop toward a hosted product. That exposed everything a polished prototype lets you ignore: stale browser chunks, lost agent sessions, long-running builds, missing model keys, worker restarts, and unclear recovery.

I added safer fallbacks, actionable errors, health checks, deployment runbooks, and stricter network boundaries. The interface also learned to keep the original artifact when a repair failed. Loopy became less magical and more useful, which was the point.

title: I called it Loopy
dek: The old name described infrastructure. The new one described how I wanted teams to work.
body: Plumbline sounded precise, but it made the product feel like a measuring tool. I cared about iteration: an idea takes a lap through a brief, directions, critique, a human decision, and evidence, then comes back changed. Loopy made that behavior legible. The name also kept me honest. If the product ever jumped straight from prompt to polished answer, it was betraying its own name.

title: The scorecard finally had somewhere to go
dek: Evaluation became useful once it changed the next decision. A score alone just decorated the last build.
body: I connected the brief, concept gallery, live preview, scorecard, and designer thoughts into one loop. The evaluation could now send the work somewhere: approve it, steer it with a reason, or reject it and preserve what failed.

That changed my relationship with AI output. I was no longer asking whether a screen looked good in isolation. I could ask whether it answered the brief, respected the design system, held together visually, and deserved another lap. I treated the score as evidence for a decision, not the decision itself.

title: Loopy started as a hand-built harness
dek: I built the product only after the manual loop started helping with real client work.
body: Before Loopy was an app, I conducted the process by hand.

I worked across OpenClaw, Claude Code, Cursor, prompts, skills, and plug-ins to turn fuzzy client ideas into prototypes that could be compared and tested. That beat arguing about them in the abstract.
The handoffs were clumsy, but the value was real. A brief stayed connected to the concepts. A critique could send the work back. Research could change the next attempt.
Loopy came from wanting to preserve that method without asking a client team to understand the pile of tools underneath it.

title: I started drawing with agents
dek: An editable design file gave the conversation a place to land.
body: I began using Pencil as a shared design surface with agents. Instead of asking for a mockup image, I kept the work in an editable .pen file where the hierarchy, copy, spacing, and alternatives could be inspected and changed.

The difference was small and important. I could point to a real node, ask why it existed, move it, and carry that decision into code. The design did not disappear into a screenshot or a chat transcript. That experiment became the basis for how I later designed Loopy's iteration stage and its Buzz integration.

title: I refused to pick concepts from prose
dek: Three descriptions are not three design directions if I cannot actually see or use them.
body: The StickerGiant agents were handing me concept descriptions and loose component files. I built a temporary preview that rendered A, B, and C side by side without touching the real app, then tore it down after I chose.

I also hardened the inspiration step. If the live source timed out, the system had to use a curated fallback or ask me whether to continue. It could no longer silently skip the part that kept concepts from collapsing into generic templates.
Seeing the options made me faster. Refusing invisible shortcuts made the options better.

title: I put the brief before the prompt
dek: The agents needed the client's world before they needed another instruction.
body: I added a project setup that captured the product, audience, goals, data, competitors, and constraints once. Every later brief and design agent had to read that context before making anything.

After evaluation, I could push the working build into Figma, let people annotate the canvas, and bring those notes back into the next round. The agent did the regeneration while the team kept the decision rights. That was the shape I wanted for client work.

title: I gave the agents different jobs
dek: One chat should not brainstorm, build, critique, test, and approve its own work.
body: I split the StickerGiant workflow into roles. A generator explored. A principal designer challenged the work. Separate checks looked for design-system drift and accessibility failures. The share step stayed behind a human confirmation.
The pipeline moved from brief to prototype to evaluation to a draft review. Each handoff left an artifact, so the model did not have to remember what it had meant five prompts earlier.
Specialization did not remove my judgment. It made the disagreements visible enough for me to use it.

title: The design system became an argument with receipts
dek: Extracting Figma values was easy. Preserving where they came from mattered more.
body: I turned StickerGiant's Figma tokens, components, variants, and source nodes into a versioned repository. During the work, the agent found disagreements around hover colors, radius, button states, and the focus ring.

I did not let it average the differences into something plausible. We kept node references, a source map, known discrepancies, and a changelog. Future agents had to challenge a conflicting extraction instead of quietly replacing the rule, and the design system could explain itself.

title: I gave the agent a room of its own
dek: The environment around the model started mattering as much as the prompt.
body: I moved my OpenClaw experiments into a contained local workspace with its own files, memory, and long-running services. Client project context no longer had to be pasted into a fresh chat every time I wanted help. The agent could inspect the real repository, keep a decision trail, run a prototype, and return later without reconstructing the project from scraps. That was my first real lesson in environment design: what the agent can see, what it can change, and what has to remain private.

title: Twenty-one folders taught me one thing
dek: The StickerGiant directory was full of experiments, but the folder count was not the value.
body: I counted 21 project folders: survey work, mobile navigation, component libraries, a brand playbook, typography and design reviews, post-purchase states, reviews, filters, badges, landing pages, print automation, and product video ideas.

Some had working prototypes and clear decision records. Two were basically empty. A few had polished scaffolds with the important handoff still missing. That inventory changed my standard: a project now needed a brief, an artifact I could inspect, and a record of what happened next.

title: A scaffold is not a pipeline
dek: AI can build a convincing shell long before the hard handoff works.
body: Landing Page Testing had five visible rounds tied to paid-search hypotheses. The work could be compared, critiqued, and brought back to the real design system. The Component-Library experiment looked more complete than it was: Storybook and a CLI existed, but the Figma import still ended in a placeholder alert. The separate Figma React generator folder contained nothing at all. Seeing those projects together changed what I checked first. I stopped rewarding the amount of interface around an idea and looked for the working handoff at its center.

title: I started turning decisions into systems
dek: The reusable part of a design decision is the rule and the evidence behind it.
body: For the PLP badge work, I compared semantic color systems, stress-tested them against light, dark, warm, and holographic product images, and worked through stacking and mobile behavior before recommending a direction.

I put the source-verified design tokens and component rules into a machine-readable file with Figma node references. I also built a small deploy watcher so an agent could hand a review build to a local service through a simple manifest, with failures kept for inspection. That made the next screen cheaper to reason about.

title: Product education belongs in the interaction
dek: Customers should not need a support article to understand the choice in front of them.
body: I prototyped a responsive product-list filter with product counts, active chips, unavailable choices, a clear zero state, and a mobile drawer. I also built a material tab concept that paired product specifications with a video-player shell.

Both were about the same job: helping a customer understand the catalog while they were making a choice. The filter used sample product data. The video slots were still placeholders. I left those limits visible and did not call the work production-ready.
A prototype can create value before it ships if it makes the decision easier to review.

title: The review stopped being a vibe
dek: I wanted critique that engineering could use, including the moments when Figma was wrong.
body: I compared Figma, staging captures, and computed CSS for a blog listing and the custom-sticker PDP. The reports ranked issues, separated token drift from layout problems, and called out cases where the implementation was better than the design file.

The same directory contains a project-template folder for local agent instructions. Not every idea survived: the accordion folder never became more than an empty README. A useful record shows the unfinished work too.

title: I connected AI art to print production
dek: A generated image was not a sticker until the manufacturing rules came with it.
body: I built a workflow that took a text prompt, generated artwork, and produced an Illustrator script with a CMYK document, bleed, and a named cut-line layer.
The same tool could run from the command line or behind an HTTP request.

I studied an existing Illustrator MCP bridge to understand the interactive path, but I did not write that server. My generator used direct local scripts and could capture the Illustrator result for review.
The generated image was only the first half of the job. The production constraints made it reviewable by manufacturing.

title: The agent learned to say what it could not see
dek: A confident design review is dangerous when the source API did not expose the thing being reviewed.
body: I used a Figma review to inspect PDP and legacy layouts for layer naming, responsive sizing, variables, and typography. The report turned the findings into code-generation actions, not a vague list of best practices. It also recorded which color and type bindings the available metadata could not verify. The agent had to separate observation from inference, so the client team could act on what was proven and check the rest themselves.

title: I designed the states the ticket left out
dek: The happy path was one screen. The real customer experience was several different products hiding inside it.
body: For the post-purchase account prompt, I split the experience into an unknown guest, a known guest, and a logged-in customer. Each state needed its own copy, validation, loading, error, and escape behavior.

The product-review work had a similar problem. Replacing the old nested-scroll widget meant designing an exposed section with rating filters, verified-customer context, business responses, and accessible reading order.

AI helped me enumerate the states quickly. Both pieces remained coded prototypes: the forms, review data, and backend connections were mocked. The design work was deciding which differences mattered to a real customer.

title: Brand rules became something agents could query
dek: A PDF tells people what the brand was. A shared source can help people and agents keep using it.
body: I rebuilt the StickerGiant brand playbook as one set of structured rules served through a website, a small command-line tool, and a Git-backed editor. A person could browse it. An agent could search it, validate colors, or compile guidance for a channel.

A typography audit exposed the same need in the design system. Base styles, utility classes, prose rules, and responsive overrides were all trying to own heading size. The goal was consistency without depending on everyone's memory.

title: The first useful outputs were review surfaces
dek: AI was most helpful when it made existing client evidence easier to see and discuss.
body: I returned to three early StickerGiant experiments. Survey data became a dashboard with charts, sentiment, action items, and a printable report. The mobile homepage became a working Figma reconstruction so navigation and local assets could be reviewed as behavior.

I also experimented with a Figma-connected component library and Storybook to make button states inspectable. The code did not prove production adoption, but it gave the team a surface for discussing what the design actually meant.
That became a pattern in my client work: use AI to shorten the distance between evidence and a decision, not to manufacture certainty.
